background.definition: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) is defined as a disease state characterized by airflow limitation that is usually progressive and associated with an abnormal inflammatory response of the lung to noxious particles or gases. Some patients have significant extrapulmonary effects (e.g., cardiac) that may contribute to disease severity. Management of chronic COPD is covered in the EE+ chapter on chronic management of COPD. a73 An acute exacerbation of COPD is defined as an acute event occurring over <14 days and characterized by a worsening, beyond daily variation, of the patient's respiratory symptoms (dyspnea and/or cough and sputum production) and may be accompanied by tachypnea and/or tachycardia. Frequent exacerbations are defined as 2 or more per year. Exacerbations not only negatively affect quality of life but are associated with an acceleration of lung function decline and increased mortality. GOLD 2026 noted that evidence from observational studies show that even one moderate or severe exacerbation prior to initiating maintenance pharmacological therapy increases risk of subsequent events; they recommend using a threshold of one moderate exacerbation to consider treatment escalation.

list.listitem: In the Canadian Optimal Therapy of COPD Trial, there were 0.85 exacerbations per patient year.

Based on records from 610 subjects in the National Emphysema Treatment Trial, 26% had an acute exacerbation over a 1-year follow-up. The annual rate of acute exacerbations varies greatly across trials, with some reporting an exacerbation in up to 64% of patients.

In a systematic review, patients with mild COPD had a mean of 0.8 exacerbations per year with rates increasing in patients with moderate, severe, and very severe disease (1.2, 1.6, and 2.0, respectively).

In 2000, patients with COPD had 8 million physician outpatient visits, 1.5 million emergency department (ED) visits, and 726,000 hospitalizations. Data were similar for 2009, with 8 million office visits, 1.5 million ED visits, and 715,000 hospitalizations.
In 2010, US costs for COPD were projected to be approximately $49.9 billion, including $29.5 billion in direct healthcare costs.

Based on data from the National Center for Chronic Disease Prevention and Health Promotion, the CDC reported 165,248 (5.44 per 1,000 Medicare enrollees aged ≥65 years) hospitalizations with COPD as the first-listed diagnosis.

Chronic lower respiratory disease, including COPD, was the fifth leading cause of death in the US in 2023 accounting for 4.7% of total deaths. Over 140,000 Americans die each year from COPD. In 2020, the age-standardized death rate in patients over age 44 years was 116.2/100,000 for men and 98/100,000 for women (Centers for Disease Control).
COPD exacerbations cause frequent hospital admissions, contribute to hospital or early post-discharge death, reduce quality of life, and hasten a progressive decline in pulmonary function.
Based on a report by the American Lung Association using Healthcare Cost and Utilization Project (H-CUP) data, there were more than 335,000 COPD hospitalizations in 2020.
In a three-year observational study, 31% of 2,138 patients with COPD reported a total of 1,452 COPD exacerbations requiring hospital admission during the study period.

In patients with an acute exacerbation of COPD, the prevalence of concomitant pulmonary embolus (PE) and deep vein thrombosis was 17.2% (95% CI 13.4%-21.3%) and 7.1% (95% CI 3.7%-11.4%%), respectively, based on a meta-analysis of 17 studies including 3170 patients. Associated factors for PE were dyspnea, pleuritic chest pain, lower limb asymmetry or edema, higher heart rates, and longer hospital stays. A second meta-analysis of 16 studies including 5035 patients found a lower prevalence of PE in acute exacerbation of COPD of 12.9% (95% CI: 8.9%-18.4%), noting a higher prevalence in studies in which all patients underwent CT vs. those in which CT was carried out only after screening patients based on study-specific diagnostic protocols (19.4% vs. 7.8%).

COPD exacerbations appear to increase the risk of cardiovascular events within 1-3 months. Authors of a systematic review and meta-analysis of 8 studies found an increased risk of stroke (6 studies; RR 1.7, 95% CI 1.2-2.4) and acute myocardial infarction (6 studies; RR 2.4, 95% CI = 1.4-4.2) within a few months following a COPD exacerbation.

The pooled prevalence of arrhythmias in patients with an acute COPD exacerbation was 15% (95% CI: 12-18%) in a meta-analysis of 28 studies. Arrhythmias were significantly associated with increased in-hospital mortality (RR 3.33, 95% CI 3.27-3.38).
Heightened relative rates for cardiovascular events remain beyond one year following an acute exacerbation of COPD irrespective of severity (aHR, 1.8, 95% CI 1.8-1.9).
A combination of environmental and genetic factors is implicated in the cause of COPD.
Cigarette smoking and passive exposure to cigarette smoke are the largest contributors along with occupational exposure (attributable risk about 19%), genetics and lung growth and development.

Exacerbations are most commonly triggered by respiratory infections (most often viral [rhinovirus], bacterial, or occasionally fungal [particularly Aspergillus species]) but can also be precipitated by allergens, air pollution, wildfire smoke and dust storms; a cause cannot be determined for about one-third of episodes. Other causes of exacerbations include heart failure, pulmonary embolism, non-respiratory infection, and pneumothorax.
Authors of the cited review detailed the detrimental impact of air pollution exposure on COPD pathophysiology that may increase a patient’s susceptibility to air pollution.
Authors of a meta-analysis of 19 studies found psychological distress increased risk of acute exacerbation of COPD, COPD-related hospitalization, and death.

In a study of risk factors for COPD exacerbation among 1528 participants in the Genetic Epidemiology of COPD Study (COPDGene) without a history of exacerbation in the previous year, investigators found 33.2% (n=508) had at least one moderate or severe exacerbation in the 36 months studied. Gastroesophageal reflux disease, chronic bronchitis, high symptom burden (measured by Modified Medical Research Council Dyspnea Scale and COPD Assessment Test), and lower FEV1% predicted were associated with increased risk of exacerbation. For each 1-point increase in graduated risk score, investigators found a 25-30% increase in exacerbation rate over the study duration.

Oxidative stress may be an important amplifying mechanism in both development of COPD and exacerbations. In addition, there appears to be an imbalance between proteases and antiproteases in the lungs of patients with COPD.

Investigation is underway to identify distinct etioendophenotypes for developing novel and targeted therapies by incorporating traits of the acute event and of patients who experience recurrent events.

The pathologic changes of COPD include chronic inflammation and structural changes in the lung from repeated injury and repair (see Chronic COPD). An acute exacerbation is associated with increased airway inflammation, increased mucus production and marked gas trapping.

Endothelial function, in particular endothelium-dependent and independent vasodilation, is significantly impaired during a COPD exacerbation compared to recovery/stable COPD. This could in part explain the increased risk of cardiovascular events following a COPD exacerbation.

Acute exacerbations of COPD are associated with increased hyaluronidase activity and subsequent degradation of hyaluronic acid, which may contribute to airway inflammation and subsequent lung function decline during exacerbations. Bacterial-related COPD exacerbations have also been associated with an increase in neutrophils, eosinophils, tumor necrosis factor alpha, and interleukin 1.

The most common viruses isolated during and shortly after an exacerbation according to GOLD 2026 are human rhinovirus, influenza, para-influenza and metapneumovirus; exacerbations associated with viral infections are often more severe. Infection is present in about 50%; the usual organisms are Haemophilus influenzae, Streptococcus pneumoniae, and Moraxella catarrhalis. Aspergillus species may be identified in patients with moderate or severe exacerbations.

Excessive prostaglandin production can increase susceptibility to infection associated with COPD exacerbations and promote inadequate alveolar repair. Inhibition of endogenous prostanoid synthesis or signaling may have therapeutic potential.

list.listitem: Smoking cessation has the greatest capacity to alter the course of COPD and reduces the frequency of COPD exacerbations; A even living in communities with smoke-free public laws/regulations appears to reduce COPD hospitalizations. C
Influenza vaccination can reduce serious illness in patients with COPD and likely reduces COPD exacerbations. B

Interventions that reduce frequency of exacerbations include bronchodilators, inhaled corticosteroid-containing regimens, non-steroidal anti-inflammatory agents (roflumilast, dupilumab, mepolizumab), anti-infectives (vaccines, long-term macrolides), mucoregulators (N-acetylcysteine, carbocysteine, erdosteine), vitamin D, cineole (the main constituent of eucalyptus oil), smoking cessation, shielding measures (e.g., mask wearing, hand washing), pulmonary rehabilitation, and lung-volume reduction. A GOLD 2026 Some of these interventions are also discussed in the chapter on chronic COPD management.

The combination of a long-acting inhaled beta-agonist (LABA) and a long-acting muscarinic antagonist (LAMA) is recommended in those with frequent exacerbations. Adding inhaled corticosteroid (ICS) for patients with stage III or IV COPD and in those with repeated exacerbations reduces COPD exacerbations, especially in those with eosinophil counts >100 cells/microL. A

Inhaled LABA + LAMA may be associated with a lower risk of COPD exacerbation and with greater improvement in FEV1 than LABA + ICS combination without differences in the incidence of serious severe adverse events or quality of life. B
Combination self-management interventions are associated with a lower probability of respiratory-related hospitalization. B
Primary prevention is discussed in the chapter on chronic COPD management.

Please see bottom line (above) and the chapter on Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease (chronic management) for additional discussion of use of medications to prevent exacerbations and manage symptoms.

Smoking cessation in patients with asymptomatic airway obstruction reduced all-cause mortality in the group receiving a smoking intervention in one randomized clinical trial (RCT). Pharmacotherapy for smoking cessation (nicotine replacement, varenicline, bupropion, and nortriptyline) and counseling should be offered if appropriate.
Living in a community with a comprehensive smoke-free law or regulation reduced COPD hospitalizations by 22% compared to living in a community with a moderate-weak law or no law.

GOLD 2026 recommends that all patients with COPD receive all recommended vaccinations including yearly influenza vaccination B, COVID-19 B, pneumococcal vaccine (PCV20 or PCV21; B ), respiratory syncytial virus if over age 49 years A, Tdap if not vaccinated in adolescence B, and zoster vaccine if over age 50 years.

Influenza vaccination can reduce the number of COPD exacerbations and hospitalizations. In one study of 87 patients, the absolute risk reductions for acute exacerbations in 1 year were 9.6, 23.6, and 24.7 per 100 person-years in patients with mild, moderate, and severe COPD, respectively. There were also 10 fewer hospitalizations for these patients in the year after vaccination.

Authors of an updated Cochrane review of 12 trials found that pneumococcal vaccination for individuals with COPD reduced the likelihood of developing community-acquired pneumonia (odds ratio [OR] 0.59; 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.41-0.85) and the likelihood of a COPD exacerbation (OR 0.60; 95% CI 0.39-0.93). There was no effect on hospitalizations or all-cause mortality.
Pneumococcal vaccination is recommended for patients with COPD age 65 years or older or for younger patients who have significant comorbid conditions.

A vaccine containing surface proteins from non-typeable H. influenzae and Moraxella catarrhalis administered to patients with COPD did not reduce the yearly rate of moderate or severe exacerbations based on an RCT of 606 adults with stable COPD and moderate-to-very severe airflow limitation. The vaccine might be helpful for preventing severe exacerbations in patients with frequent exacerbations who are taking ICS at baseline.

ACCP/ATS recommend PR for patients with moderate to very-severe COPD who have had a recent exacerbation (4 or fewer weeks) to prevent exacerbations; PR is not suggested for those with more remote exacerbations.

ACCP/ATS recommend education and case management, including direct access to a health-care specialist at least monthly, to prevent hospitalization for patients with COPD and a previous or recent history of exacerbations. They also suggest education with a written action plan and case management for the prevention of severe acute exacerbations in patients with COPD.

Although data on self-management are conflicting, authors of an updated Cochrane review of 7 RCTs found that action plans with limited COPD education and ongoing support improved recognition of and response to an exacerbation with initiation of antibiotics and corticosteroids and reduced combined hospitalizations and ED visits over 12 months.

Authors of a second Cochrane review of self-management interventions that include a COPD action plan found a lower probability of respiratory-related hospitalization (OR 0.69; 95% CI 0.51-0.94) but no significant effect from self‐management on number of COPD exacerbations or all‐cause mortality.

In an evidence review, authors concluded that there was little evidence of benefit of providing self-management support to patients shortly after hospital discharge, although there might be a reduction in hospital admissions and improvement in health-related quality of life.

An integrative approach to care with trained general practitioners, practice nurses, and specialized physiotherapists was not effective in improving health status or reducing exacerbations or hospital days over usual care in a practice-based study of 1086 patients with COPD. In another study, protocol-based care management delivered by medical assistants did not reduce all-cause hospitalizations, although there were some positive effects on quality of life measures.

However, in a RCT of patients hospitalized with COPD at a single institution, a 3-month nurse-administered program combining transition and long-term self-management support resulted in significantly fewer COPD-related hospitalizations and emergency department visits (0.72; 95% CI 0.45-0.97 vs. 1.40; 95% CI 1.01-1.79) and better health-related quality of life at 6 months post-discharge.

Complete a clinical assessment for potential respiratory (e.g., pneumonia) conditions, cardiovascular conditions and pulmonary embolus. C

list.listitem: Diagnostic criteria for COPD can be found in the chapter on chronic COPD management.

Assess the medical history for severity of COPD based on degree of airflow limitation, duration of worsening or new symptoms, number of previous exacerbations (total and hospitalizations), comorbidities, present treatment regimen, and previous use of mechanical ventilation.

By definition, an acute increase in symptoms defines an acute exacerbation; the main symptom is increased dyspnea that is often accompanied by wheezing, chest tightness, increased cough, and sputum production, a change in character (e.g., tenacity) or color of sputum, and fever. In one study of patients with acute exacerbation of COPD, 84% with purulent sputum had positive bacterial cultures compared with only 38% who had mucoid sputum.

While dyspnea is a defining feature of an acute exacerbation, also assess patients for pain. Authors of a meta-analysis of 4 studies of patients with an acute exacerbation of COPD found a pooled prevalence for dyspnea of 91% (95% CI 87%-94%) and for pain of 44% (95% CI 35%-52%).

Sputum color, assessed in the laboratory using a color chart, may be a useful predictor of bacterial count, but data are conflicting; patient assessment of sputum color does not appear to be predictive. Authors of a meta-analysis of 13 studies found sputum color had limited value as a stand-alone test in diagnosing bacterial infection in patients with COPD due to only moderate pooled sensitivity of 81% (95% CI 70-88%) and poor specificity of 50% (95% CI 35-65%).

Consider alternate diagnoses or contributors in patients presenting with suspected COPD exacerbation as noted in the differential diagnosis table. Useful differentiating features from an acute exacerbation of CHF include signs of heart failure (e.g., jugular venous distention, peripheral edema), and the overall clinical impression.
Patients can also present with many nonspecific features of acute illness including malaise, fatigue, depression, and confusion.
In patients with severe COPD, the most important sign of a severe exacerbation is a change in mental status.

GOLD guidelines recommend use of either the Medical Research Council (MRC) dyspnea scale or the COPD Assessment Test (CAT) for evaluating patients with COPD. The MRC dyspnea scale ranges from grade 1 (not troubled by dyspnea) to grade 5 (too breathless to leave the house or breathless when dressing or undressing). CAT is an eight-item questionnaire assessing and quantifying the impact of COPD symptoms on health status. In one study with 161 patients, higher baseline CAT scores were seen among those with frequent COPD exacerbations; rises in CAT score were significantly associated with falls in FEV1.

In the COPDGene study including 1,528 participants with a smoking history and COPD, an MRC score >=2 or CAT score >=10 was associated with an increased rate of moderate or severe exacerbations (RR 1.99 [1.62-2.46] and RR 2.28 [1.83–2.86], respectively).

Authors of a systematic review and meta-analysis found that CAT was a useful adjunct to clinical assessment for predicting COPD exacerbation, health status deterioration, depression, and mortality. However, the evidence did not support the recommended cutoff points of ≥10 for CAT and ≥2 for MRC as equivalents for the purpose of assessing patient symptoms.

listitem.strong: Assessment of severity of the acute exacerbation

list.listitem: Assessment of severity of illness is important for determining management, particularly whether hospitalization is needed; aspects of the clinical examination that inform this decision include use of accessory muscles of breathing, paradoxical chest wall movements, worsening or new onset central cyanosis, development of peripheral edema, or hemodynamic instability, and deteriorating mental status. Also assess patients for and signs of pneumonia.

GOLD 2026 defines the following severity classes, adapted from Rome criteria (a pocket card is available on the GOLD website listing these criteria): Mild: dyspnea visual analog scale (VAS) <5, RR <24 breaths/min, HR <95 bpm, resting oxygen saturation >=92% on ambient air (or patient’s usual oxygen prescription) AND change 3% or less if known, and CRP <10 mg/L if obtained Moderate (at least one of 5): VAS >=5, RR >=24 breaths/min, HR >=95 beats per minute, resting oxygen saturation <92% on ambient air (or patient’s usual oxygen prescription) AND/OR change >3% if known, CRP >=10 mg/L, and ABG (if obtained) may show hypoxemia (PaO2 70-80 mmHg) Severe: dyspnea, RR, HR, O2 sat and CRP as for moderate AND ABG showing showing hypoxemia (PaO2 <=60 mmHg) and/or hypercapnia (PaCO2 >45 mmHg) and acidosis (pH <7.35)

GOLD 2026 also recommends the following severity classification for hospitalized patients: No respiratory failure: respiratory rate: ≤24 breaths/min; heart rate ≤95 bpm, no use of accessory respiratory muscles; no changes in mental status; hypoxemia improved with supplemental oxygen given via Venturi mask 24-35% FiO2; no increase in PaCO2 Respiratory failure: respiratory rate: >24 breaths/min; heart rate >95 bpm, using accessory respiratory muscles; appropriate mental status; hypoxemia improved with supplemental oxygen via Venturi mask >35% FiO2; hypercapnia i.e., PaCO2 increased compared with baseline or elevated 50-60 mmHg Ventilatory failure: respiratory rate: >24 breaths/min; heart rate >95 bpm, using accessory respiratory muscles; acute changes in mental status; hypoxemia not improved with supplemental oxygen via Venturi mask or requiring FiO2 >40%; hypercapnia i.e., PaCO2 increased compared with baseline or elevated >60 mmHg and the presence of acidosis (pH ≤7.25)

A simple risk score (the BAP-65) can accurately predict hospital mortality, cost, and length of stay of an episode of acute exacerbation of COPD, with 5 severity classes based on age and three risk factors (blood urea nitrogen >25 mg/dL, altered mental status, and pulse >109 beats/minute). Mortality increased with increasing BAP-65 score, ranging from <1% in subjects with a score of 0 to >25% in those meeting all BAP-65 criteria. Similarly, need for mechanical ventilation also increased with increasing score (2% in the lowest risk cohort vs. 55% in the highest risk group).

Alternatively, in one study of 2487 patients presenting to an ED with an exacerbation of COPD, predictors of death during hospital admission or within 1 week of discharge to home from the ED were age, baseline dyspnea, previous need for long-term home oxygen therapy or non-invasive mechanical ventilation, altered mental status, and use of inspiratory accessory muscles or paradoxical breathing upon ED arrival (area under the curve (AUC) = 0.85).
Spirometry is not useful for assessing an acute exacerbation because it is difficult for a sick patient to perform and the measurements are not accurate in this setting.

Oxygen saturation measured by pulse oximetry was found in one study to be the best tool for evaluating hypoxemia. The optimal cutoff value is 88.5% or less. Pulse oximetry measurements are not as accurate as arterial blood gas and may overestimate oxygenation in patients with darker skin tones.

While not always practical in the outpatient setting, ABG measurement can be extremely useful; an acute change is more helpful than the absolute values. Respiratory failure is indicated by a PaO2 of <60 mm Hg and/or an SaO2 of <90% with or without PaCO2 >50 mm HG on room air. In addition to oxygenation and carbon dioxide retention, moderate to severe acidosis (pH <7.36) plus hypercapnia (PaCO2 >45-60 mm Hg) are indications for mechanical ventilation.

The presence of purulent sputum during an exacerbation is a sufficient indication of infection to start empiric antibiotics; Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae, and Moraxella catarrhalis are the most common pathogens; in patients at GOLD stage 3 and 4, Pseudomonas aeruginosa becomes important.
Obtain a CXR or chest CT scan to rule out alternative diagnoses (e.g., pneumonia, CHF, PE).

A low systolic blood pressure (<60 mm Hg) and inability to increase the PaO2 above 60 mm Hg despite high flow oxygen suggest PE; CXR and ECG findings in severe COPD (which may be accompanied by cor pulmonale) can confuse the diagnosis.

In addition to BNP,CXR findings (especially cardiomegaly) and the ECG (especially ST-T wave changes consistent with ischemia) can assist in distinguishing between heart failure and COPD exacerbation. GOLD guidelines also suggest a whole blood count to assess polycythemia, anemia or leukocytosis.

Ultrasound assessment of the inferior vena cava diameter successfully differentiated between pulmonary and cardiac causes of dyspnea in one prospective observational study. B-mode i values >9 mm predicted dyspnea of cardiac origin with a sensitivity of 84.4% and a specificity of 92.9% (LR+ 11.8, LR− 0.16). Similarly, in the ED setting, cardiopulmonary ultrasound had superior accuracy to clinical examination or combination "clinical examination-NT-proBNP-x-ray” (90% vs. 67% and 81%, respectively). GOLD 2026 recommends cardiac ultrasound for assessment of heart failure or suspected pneumonia or pneumothorax.
Helium 3 magnetic resonance imaging ventilation defect percentage was significantly associated with COPD exacerbations.

Based on 2 longitudinal studies - COPDGene COPD (n= 9416 adults) and the Canadian Cohort Obstructive Lung Disease (n=1561 participants) - a diagnostic strategy integrating respiratory symptoms, respiratory quality of life, spirometry, and structural lung abnormalities on CT imaging resulted in some individuals without airway obstruction being newly classified as having COPD (811/5250, 15.4%). In the former study, these individuals had an increased risk of all-cause and respiratory-related death, frequent exacerbations, and rapid lung function decline compared with individuals classified as not having COPD. In the latter study, individuals newly classified as having COPD experienced more exacerbations (adjusted incidence rate ratio, 2.09; 95% CI, 1.25-3.51). Some individuals (282/4166, 6.8%) with airflow obstruction without respiratory symptoms or evidence of structural lung disease were no longer classified as having COPD.
Clinical assessment includes presence of hemoptysis; deep vein thrombosis; and history of cancer, surgery or bone fracture. If suspected, GOLD 2026 recommends obtaining D-dimer and CT angiography.

Use of elevated BNP in patients presenting to the ED with pre-existing pulmonary disease can help distinguish between an exacerbation of heart failure versus pulmonary disease; especially useful for excluding heart failure.

In one study, use of N-terminal BNP for patients presenting with dyspnea to the ED improved accuracy of clinical judgement (BNP ≥100 pg/mL indicative of heart failure) and reduced length of the ED visit, likelihood of rehospitalization, and cost of care.

However, while authors of a systematic review of 51 studies found that natriuretic peptide levels were low in stable COPD, they were elevated in 16-60% of patients with an acute exacerbation of COPD and significantly increased in those with concomitant left ventricular systolic dysfunction or cor pulmonale. In three included studies of patients with an acute exacerbation of COPD, N terminal-proBNP >125 pg/ml occurred in 16%, 27% and 44% of patients. While this test has reasonable accuracy (negative predictive values between 0.8 and 0.98 in studies of acute exacerbation of COPD) for excluding heart failure, the high false positive rate will increase the need for further testing.
GOLD 2026 recommends obtaining both NT proBNP and BNP to assist in distinguishing heart failure from COPD exacerbation.

Several biomarkers suggest acute exacerbation and/or bacterial infection. In one study, CRP was more likely to be elevated in acute exacerbation and correlated with sputum purulence. A cluster RCT in Spain found that giving primary care doctors access to C-reactive protein results in reduced antibiotic prescribing.

A study randomized 653 patients to CRP guided or usual care. Physicians were advised that antibiotics are unlikely to be helpful if CRP is less than 20 mg/L, that antibiotics may be helpful if CRP is 20 to 40 mg/L, especially in the presence of purulent sputum, and that antibiotics are likely to be helpful if CRP is greater than 40 mg/L. The CRP guided therapy group safely reduced antibiotic use (NNT = 5 to prevent one unnecessary course of antibiotics).

Procalcitonin is a marker of bacterial infection and has been used in several studies to guide use of antibiotics successfully for lower respiratory infection, reducing use of antibiotics for patients presenting to the ED with dyspnea and cough. A value less than 0.25 ng/mL and especially less than 0.1 ng/mL suggests viral infection or no infection.

Authors of a meta-analysis of 39 papers evaluating 61 biomarkers found moderate quality evidence for associations between CRP, serum procalcitonin, sputum interleukin (IL)-8 and sputum tumor necrosis factor alpha (TNF-α) and the presence of bacterial pathogens in sputum of patients with an acute COPD exacerbation.

Procalcitonin, at a cutoff of 0.31 ng/mL, combined with CRP (cutoff 15 mg/mL) and PaCO2 (cutoff 73.5 mm Hg) were highly predictive of noninvasive ventilation failure based on a retrospective case-control study of patients with an acute exacerbation of COPD, with an area under the curve of 0.978 (95% CI 0.961-0.995).
Serum amyloid A was found in one study to predict acute exacerbation and was better at predicting event severity than CRP or procalcitonin.

Blood eosinophil count may predict increased exacerbations in patients treated with LABA without ICS. Authors of a meta-analysis of 14 cohort and 1 case-control study found that patients with an acute COPD exacerbation who had a high eosinophil count had a lower risk of mortality (RR 0.6, 95 % CI 0.5-0.8), shorter length of hospital stay, but slightly higher readmission rates (RR 1.07, 95%CI 1.01-1.13).
Additional laboratory testing should be based on co-morbidities and current medications (e.g., glucose, electrolytes).

GOLD 2026 guidelines suggest obtaining vitamin D status on all patients hospitalized for exacerbations and that those identified with severe deficiency (<10 ng/ml or <25 nM) be supplemented. Authors of a systematic review and meta-analysis of 4 RCTs found that supplementation with vitamin D in patients with vitamin D deficiency reduced the rate of moderate/severe exacerbations but had not benefit for those without vitamin D deficiency.

In an RCT including 737 patients hospitalized with acute exacerbation of COPD, active looking with D-dimer for evidence of VTE had no impact on clinical outcomes of symptomatic VTE, readmission for COPD, or death over usual care.
Validated clinical decision support tools to assist in weaning patients from mechanical ventilation include the the CROP index, and the BODE index.
The well validated DECAF score can determine mortality risk for hospitalized patients.
Another prognostic score is the BAP-65.
The risk of bad outcomes with a COPD exacerbation presenting to the ED can be predicted using the Ottawa COPD risk score.

A risk score developed in a cohort of elderly Dutch patients with a diagnosis of pneumonia, acute bronchitis, or acute exacerbation of COPD predicted their prognosis. It was validated in a. national cohort of Dutch GP patients.

The performance of artificial intelligence and machine learning models was evaluated in a systematic review and meta-analysis of 13 studies (most using electronic record or claims data). The models demonstrated moderate-to-high discriminatory accuracy in predicting COPD exacerbations and readmissions, with pooled area under the curve (AUCs) of 0.73-0.77. The authors noted high study heterogeneity, limited external validation, and frequent methodological concerns that restrict generalizability of results.
Suspect an acute exacerbation in a patient with COPD who presents with an acute change in baseline dyspnea, cough, and/or sputum that is beyond normal day-to-day variations.

Assess symptom severity, mental status and hemodynamic stability, blood gases and CXR. Consider presence of serious comorbidities and alternate or contributing diagnoses (pneumonia, heart failure, PE). If hypoxemic, administer oxygen and monitor response.
If there is increased work of breathing or impaired gas exchange, consider NIV and hospital admission where proper care and monitoring can be provided.
Consider appropriate place of care based on presence of home support, response to initial management and indications for hospitalization and medical ICU listed below.
Treatment goals are to resolve the current episode, minimize its negative effects and prevent future exacerbations

A For patients with hypercarbic respiratory failure or those not responding to HFNT, use NIV to improve gas exchange and reduce work of breathing and need for intubation. They also decrease hospital duration and improve survival.
Optimize management of comorbidities. C

Pulmonary rehabilitation following an acute exacerbation of COPD is highly effective in reducing the number of subsequent hospital admissions and mortality and improving health-related quality of life. A

Short-acting inhaled bronchodilators are recommended for symptom control; GOLD 2026 guidelines favor beta-2-agonists with or without anticholinergic agents while the American College of Physicians recommends beginning with anticholinergic agents. These can be delivered via metered dose inhalers or nebulizers. GOLD 2026 recommends one dose of nebulized medication every hour for 2-3 doses or a pMDI one or two puffs every one hour for two or three doses and then every 2-4 hours based on the patient’s response.

GOLD 2026 guidelines also recommend consideration of continuing or beginning long-acting inhaled bronchodilators (either beta2-agonists or anticholinergic agents or both) once the patient has stabilized, prior to discharge. Use spacers or air-driven nebulizers when appropriate.

Based on a retrospective analysis of registry and claims databases including 25,603 patients with COPD who initiated single-inhaler triple therapy with budesonide/glycopyrrolate/formoterol fumarate within 1-year of a COPD exacerbation, initiation within 30 days of the exacerbation lowered the risk of subsequent annualized exacerbations and risk of cardiopulmonary events compared to delayed and very delayed initiators (181-365 days).

GOLD 2026 guidelines recommend consideration of oral corticosteroids for severe exacerbations. Prednisone 40 mg for 5 days can shorten recovery time and hospital length of stay. ACCP/ATS do not recommend oral steroids for the sole purpose of preventing hospitalization due to subsequent acute exacerbations of COPD beyond the first 30 days following the initial acute exacerbation of COPD.

Systemic steroids have been shown to reduce the likelihood of treatment failure and decrease hospital length of stay by 1.4 days for hospitalized patients with an acute exacerbation of COPD. In a Cochrane review, oral or parenteral steroid treatment reduced the likelihood of treatment failure (NNT 10) and the duration of hospitalization (−1.2 days) compared with placebo. There was no difference in mortality and there was an increased risk of adverse events with steroid treatment (NNTH 5), including pneumonia.

In a meta-analysis of 68 RCTs, investigators found that systemic corticosteroid treatment of any duration for an acute COPD exacerbation, regardless of severity, was associated with less frequent treatment failure but higher rates of adverse effects, based on low-quality evidence.

A 5-day course of systemic corticosteroids (40 mg daily, with the first dose given IV and subsequent doses given orally) was found to be as effective as a 14-day course in a randomized controlled trial amongst 314 patients with an acute exacerbation of COPD. Longer courses of steroids are associated with increased 1-year risk of pneumonia hospitalization (adjusted hazard ratio [aHR] 1.2; 95% CI 1.0-1.3) and all-cause mortality (aHR 1.8; 95% CI 1.5-2.2), based on a nationwide observational cohort study of 10,152 outpatients of median age 70 years with COPD.

Authors of a Cochrane review of 8 studies with 582 patients found no increase in treatment failure with shorter duration (7 or fewer days) corticosteroid treatment compared with longer treatment durations (typically 10-14 days). There were no differences in adverse events or hospital length of stay. They concluded that for most patients, 5 days is optimal.

This finding was supported in an analysis of pooled individual patient data from two RCTs on corticosteroid-sparing regimens including 632 patients with an acute exacerbation of COPD. This study found longer hospital stays (mean difference, 5.4 days) and fewer days alive and out of hospital within 14 days (4.2 vs. 8.4 days) comparing the 14-day regimen with the 2-5-day regimen group. There were no differences in the composite endpoint 'death or ICU admission' or mortality risk during the 6-month follow-up period. Patients randomized to the 14-day regimen, however, were older, less often received pre-treatment antibiotics and more often received pre-treatment with systemic corticosteroids.

Oral steroids are as effective as IV steroids for patients with a non-severe exacerbation of COPD. In a retrospective study of non-critically ill patients with a COPD exacerbation, low dose oral steroids (maximum dose between 20 and 80 mg oral prednisone within the first 2 days of hospitalization) performed as well as high-dose IV steroids (maximum dose between 120 and 800 mg of equivalent intravenous dose of prednisone during the first 2 days of hospitalization) with respect to treatment failure and were associated with shorter length of stay and lower cost.

Steroids may be less effective in treating COPD exacerbations in patient with low blood eosinophils, but further study is needed. In a multi-center RCT of 318 patients admitted with acute exacerbation of COPD in Denmark, eosinophil-guided therapy was non-inferior to standard therapy with systemic corticosteroids for treatment failure (26% in each group) and reduced steroid exposure, but numbers were too small to determine potential harm which included a non-significantly greater number of deaths at 30 days in the intervention group (6% vs. 4%).

In a UK trial (STARR-2), 308 adults with a history of at least one exacerbation in the previous 12 months requiring systemic corticosteroids with or without antibiotics were recruited from 14 primary care practices. Of the 93 who had an acute exacerbation during the study period (114 total exacerbations), blood eosinophil-directed therapy (30 mg prednisone once daily for those with a blood eosinophil count >=2%) was non-inferior to standard care with same prednisone dose with respect to treatment failure rate (19% vs. 32%; RR 0.6, 95% CI 0.3-1.04) and hospital admission for COPD exacerbation (2/102 vs. 1/101). All patients were also prescribed antibiotics.

Authors of a meta-analysis of 20 RCTs patients with moderate or severe exacerbations found noninferiority of inhaled vs. systemic corticosteroids with respect to treatment failure rate (RR 1.8, 95% CI 0.8-4.0, n=569 participants), breathlessness, or serious adverse events (RR 1.5, 95% CI 0.6-3.9, n=246) based on low certainty evidence. Hyperglycemia was more common among those randomized to systemic steroids and oral fungal infections were observed more frequently with inhaled corticosteroids.
GOLD 2026 notes that nebulized budesonide alone may be a suitable alternative for treatment of exacerbations in some patients.

GOLD 2026 guidelines recommend antibiotics, given orally if possible, for 5 days for patients with acute exacerbation of COPD who have at least two of the following symptoms—increased dyspnea, fever, sputum volume, and sputum purulence; prior positive sputum culture during a prior exacerbation, or require mechanical ventilation (invasive or non-invasive). GOLD does not recommend particular antibiotics, and decisions should be based on local bacterial resistance patterns. Options for empiric treatment include an aminopenicillin with clavulanic acid, macrolide, tetracycline or, in selected patients, quinolone. In one RCT, use of amoxicillin was comparable to azithromycin.

Authors of a Cochrane review found that for outpatients with a mild-moderate COPD exacerbation, antibiotics reduced treatment failures from 295 to 212 per 1000 (95% CI 165-277), based on low-quality evidence. Antibiotics were not of benefit for inpatients with severe exacerbations (i.e., for inpatients excluding ICU patients; RR 0.65; 95% CI 0.38-1.12), but the effect was statistically significant when trials included older antibiotics no longer in clinical use.

In the single trial conducted in an ICU setting, antibiotic use reduced treatment failures from 565 to 107 per 1000 treated participants, (95% CI 45-254), mortality (OR 0.21; 95% CI 0.06-0.72) and hospital length of stay (MD -9.60 days; 95% CI -12.84 to -6.36).

In a meta-analysis of 68 RCTs, investigators found that antibiotic treatment of an acute exacerbation, regardless of severity, doubled the likelihood of resolution by the end of treatment (OR 2.03; 95% CI 1.47-2.80) and reduced the likelihood of treatment failure by half (OR 0.54; 95% CI 0.34-0.86), based on moderate strength evidence.

ACP also recommends limiting antibiotic treatment duration to 5 days when managing patients with COPD exacerbations and clinical evidence of bacterial infection, as above. In a meta-analysis of 21 studies, a short course of 5 days of antibiotics was as effective as longer courses in the treatment of acute exacerbation of COPD. Drugs studied included macrolides, respiratory quinolones, cephalosporins, and amoxicillin/clavulanic acid.

Extended antibiotic treatment could be considered in high-risk patients. In an RCT of 301 patients with a smoking history and at least one prior exacerbation within the past year currently admitted with an acute COPD exacerbation, initiation of 500 mg of azithromycin for 3 days in addition to standard treatment with steroids and antibiotics and continued at 250 mg every 2 days for 3 months resulted in significantly lower rates of treatment intensification (47% vs. 60%) and step-up in hospital care (13% vs. 28%) within 3 months. Although not statistically significant, mortality rates were 2% vs. 4%, respectively.
Among patients with mild to moderate COPD who have an exacerbation, those with purulent sputum and a C-reactive protein level >40 mg/L should also be considered for antibiotic treatment.

In two RCTs, giving physicians access to CRP results (not helpful if CRP <20 mg/L, helpful if CRP >40 mg/L) for hospitalized patients or outpatients with a COPD exacerbation reduced antibiotic prescribing by 15% and 20%, respectively, without increasing rates of treatment failure (44.5% vs. 45.5% among hospitalized patients) and no evidence of harm; NNT = 5 to safely reduce antibiotic use based on the most recent trial.

Similar results of decreased antibiotic prescribing with no differences in treatment failure or exacerbation recurrence were demonstrated using high procalcitonin as the biomarker of infection in a systematic review of 8 low- to moderate-quality trials with 1062 patients. However, procalcitonin testing may be more expensive than CRP and, among patients admitted to the ICU, use of a procalcitonin-based algorithm for antibiotic prescribing resulted in a higher 3-month mortality rate of 20% vs. 14%.
GOLD guidelines recommend against use of intravenous methylxanthines due to significant side effects.

Authors of a meta-analysis of 24 RCTs including 2192 patients with COPD exacerbations found that mucolytics increased treatment success (RR 1.37, 95% CI 1.08-1.73) and demonstrated benefit on overall symptom scores and presence of cough at follow-up (RR 1.93, 95% CI 1.15-3.23).

Authors of a meta-analysis of 38 RCTs comparing a Chinese medicine herbal formula Xiaoqinglong decoction with conventional therapy in patients with an acute exacerbation of COPD found the herbal therapy superior with respect to symptom improvement with no difference in rates of adverse effects. Authors of a network meta-analysis found best results on clinical efficacy or hospital length of stay from adjunctive treatment with Dengzhanxixin injection, Reduning injection, and Shengmai injection.

Use of Suhuang zhike capsule adjuvant treatment for an acute exacerbation of COPD improved clinical efficacy and reduced 1-year recurrence based on a meta-analysis of 13 RCTs including 1195 patients. Similarly, authors of a meta-analysis of 9 trials including 1591 patients found that Chinese herbal medicine as an adjunct to usual treatment for an acute COPD exacerbation significantly reduced symptom score and hospital length of stay and improved clinical effectiveness.

In an RCT including 72 hospitalized patients with acute COPD exacerbation, acupuncture compared to sham treatment or standard of care reduced dyspnea intensity on the modified Borg scale from the first day of evaluation after treatment until day 3 after treatment.

Authors of a meta-analysis of 12 studies with 915 patients found limited benefit of adjunctive acupuncture, primarily improved quality of life, but no significant differences in exercise capacity, hospitalization duration or dyspnea.

Pulmonary rehabilitation (PR) following an acute exacerbation of COPD appears to be effective in reducing the number of hospital admissions over 25 weeks (NNT 4) and mortality (NNT 6), There was also an improvement in health-related quality of life.

Authors of a meta-analysis of 20 RCTs including 1274 participants hospitalized with acute exacerbation of COPD found that early PR, started in hospital, vs. usual care showed a significantly improved readmission rate (10 trials, risk ratio 0.68, 95% CI 0.50-0.92), 6-minute walking distance (12 trials, MD 59.73, 95% CI 36.34-83.12), St George's Respiratory Questionnaire score (eight trials, MD -10.65, 95% CI -14.78 to -6.52), Borg score (eight trials, MD -0.79, 95% CI -1.26 to -0.32), and modified Medical Research Council dyspnea scale (eight trials, MD -0.38, 95% CI -0.5 to -0.25). No significant difference in mortality was found.

A meta-analysis of 17 studies from 2015-2023 evaluating PR initiated within 3 weeks of hospital discharge but not solely completed during hospital stay confirmed these results on reduced readmission rates, improved walking distance and improvements in dyspnea scales with no significant difference in mortality.

GOLD 2026 guidelines recommend giving supplemental oxygen if the patient is hypoxic (PaO2 <60 mm Hg or SaO2 <90%); oxygen is titrated to a PaO2 >60 mm Hg or SaO2 target of 88% to 92%. Venturi masks offer more accurate delivery of oxygen than nasal prongs.

The American Thoracic Society (ATS) 2020 guidelines define severe hypoxia as having PaO2 of 55 mm Hg (7.3 kPa) or lower, or SpO2 at 88% or lower as measured by pulse oximetry. In patients with edema, hematocrit of 55% or greater, or P pulmonale on ECG, the ATS defined severe hypoxia as PaO2 between 56 and 59 mm Hg (7.5-7.9 kPa) or SpO2 at 89%. For patients with COPD or interstitial lung disease and severe hypoxia, they recommend long-term home oxygen. The ATS recommends portable oxygen for ambulatory patients who desaturate during exertion. They also recommend using liquid oxygen for ambulatory patients who need higher oxygen flow rates.

Automated oxygen administration, based on a patient's peripheral oxygen saturation, appears to reduce breathing discomfort and improve physical perception of dyspnea in patients admitted with an acute COPD exacerbation, but did improve emotional status or other COPD symptoms in an RCT including 127 of 157 patients randomized.

A Swedish trial randomized 241 adults with COPD requiring oxygen to 24 vs 15 hours per day. Adherence was good. They found that using oxygen for 15 hours was as effective as 24 hours at preventing hospitalization or death in patients with severe hypoxemia.
Use of heliox, while improving respiratory acidosis and encephalopathy, does not prevent NIV failure in patients with severe COPD exacerbations.

High-flow oxygen can be considered for patients with acute hypoxemic respiratory failure, but evidence does not support a reduced need for mechanical ventilation (OR 0.79; 95% CI 0.60-1.04) or mortality benefit (OR 0.89; 95% CI 0.62-127) based on a meta-analysis of 8 RCTs with 1,818 patients.

GOLD 2026 lists indications for HFNT as at least one of the following: persistent hypoxemia, unable to tolerate or contraindication for NIV, weaning off supplemental oxygen following NIV, preventing reintubation in patients requiring intubation and positive pressure ventilation and treatment of patients with stable COPD at risk of exacerbation.

Authors of a systematic review and meta-analysis of 40 RCTs with 3597 patients with an acute exacerbation of COPD found that while HFNT did not reduce NIV intubation rates, using settings of 20-30L/minute significantly reduced PaCO2, improved pH, and lowered incidence of nasal and facial injuries. At higher settings (30-50L/minute), there was a significantly shortened hospital stay. These authors recommended low-flow settings as the preferred initial strategy.

Following extubation, authors of a meta-analysis of 8 studies including 612 patients with acute exacerbation of COPD found no differences between high-flow nasal oxygen therapy and noninvasive mechanical ventilation (NIV) on reintubation (RR 1.49, 95% CI 0.95 to 2.33). However, NIV vs. high flow oxygen significantly reduced reintubation among patients without hypercapnia.

Authors of another meta-analysis comparing high-flow oxygen vs. NIV also found no differences in patients with COPD under initial respiratory support and postextubation in either risk of intubation (RR 0.84, 95% CI 0.4 to 2; 2 RCTs with 122 patients) or reintubation (RR 1.4, 95% CI 0.7 to 2.5; 7 RCTs with 502 patients). When used for initial support for patients with an acute COPD exacerbation compared to NIV, there was also no difference in reducing treatment failure based on 2 studies. Patients undergoing HFNT had a lower incidence of facial skin breakdown but no difference in pneumothorax.

In the most recent RCT conducted in Brazil comparing HFNT with NIV in 1776 patients with acute respiratory failure who completed the study, among those in the COPD exacerbation with respiratory acidosis group (n=77), the number of patients experiencing the primary outcome of endotracheal intubation or death at 7 days was similar (10/35, 28.6% in the HFNT group vs. 11/42, 26.2% in the NIV group). The incidence of serious adverse events was similar (9.4% in the HFNT group vs. 9.9% in the NIV group).

GOLD 2026 guidelines recommend NIV as the first mode of ventilation in patients with acute respiratory failure unless contraindicated. One of the following is listed as an indication for NIV in GOLD 2026: respiratory acidosis, severe dyspnea with clinical signs of respiratory fatigue or increased work of breathing, or persistent hypoxemia despite supplemental oxygen.

NIV has a success rate of 80% to 85% and has been shown in patients with severe exacerbations to improve respiratory acidosis, decrease need for intubation, and reduce hospital length of stay and mortality.

Authors of a Cochrane review of 17 RCTs with 1264 subjects with acute hypercapnic respiratory failure due to an acute exacerbation of COPD found NIV decreased mortality risk (risk ratio [RR] 0.54; 95% CI 0.38-0.76; NNT 12) and decreased the risk of needing endotracheal intubation (RR 0.36; 95% CI 0.28-0.46; NNT 5).

Compared to invasive mechanical ventilation, NIV decreases mortality, ventilator-associated pneumonia, length of ICU and hospital stay and duration of ventilation, and rates of tracheostomy and re-intubation.

In patients with persistent hypercapnia after an acute COPD exacerbation, discharge on oxygen plus NIV compared to oxygen alone reduced annual COPD exacerbations (3.8 vs. 5.1), slightly improved health-related quality of life at 6 weeks and 3 months, prolonged time to readmission or death (4.3 vs. 1.4 months) and reduced the risk of readmission of death within 12 months (63.4% vs. 80.4%), although not overall mortality. NNT was 6 to prevent one readmission.

In a prospective study including 39 patients who were admitted to the emergency department with a diagnosis of mild-moderate hypercapnic COPD exacerbation and treated with either EzPAP, a device that enhances positive end-expiratory pressure, or NIV, EzPAP use resulted in more rapid improvement at 24 hours of oxygen saturation and respiratory acidosis.
GOLD 2026 guidelines note that NIV can be directly discontinued without weaning if the patient is improved and can tolerate at least 4 hours of unassisted breathing.

GOLD 2026 guidelines recommend invasive mechanical ventilation in patients who do not tolerate or respond to HFNT or NIV; following cardiac or respiratory arrest; diminished consciousness or psychomotor agitation inadequately controlled by sedation; massive aspiration, persistent vomiting or inability to remove respiratory secretions; severe unresponsive hemodynamic instability; or severe ventricular or supraventricular arrythmia.

In a single-site RCT including 240 patients hospitalized for an acute exacerbation of COPD, a 3-month program that combined transition and long-term self-management support resulted in significantly more COPD-related hospitalizations and emergency department visits, without improvement in quality of life.

Non-pharmacologic therapies that improve breathlessness in patients with severe disease include neuro-electrical muscle stimulation and chest wall vibration, based on strong evidence, and walking aids and breathing training, as noted above, based on moderate strength of evidence. Acupuncture/acupressure may be helpful, based on limited evidence.

Authors of a meta-analysis of 13 studies including 756 patients found that high-frequency chest wall oscillation compared to other airway clearance techniques, significantly increased expectorated sputum volume and shortened hospital stay by 4.4 days (95% CI -7.7 to -1.05; I2 = 84%).

Use of a clinical pathway in the care of patients hospitalized with a COPD exacerbation may reduce complications, readmissions, and length of stay based on a meta-analysis of 13 low-quality studies, but did not influence mortality or quality of life.

GOLD 2026 guidelines recommend hospital assessment or admission for patients with signs and symptoms of respiratory failure (eg, worsening of hypoxemia and/or hypercarbia, increased respiratory rate, use of accessory muscles, mental status changes), failure of an exacerbation to respond to initial medical management, presence of serious comorbidities (e.g., newly occurring arrhythmias), or insufficient home support. More than 80% of exacerbations can be managed as an outpatient.

GOLD 2026 notes that for monitoring gas exchange variables, the gold standard continues to be determination of ABGs in more severe cases. The use of transcutaneous capnography can be helpful in less severe cases. Oxygen saturation has been shown to be less accurate in individuals with darker skin tone.

GOLD 2026 also recommends that hospitalized patients be assessed for severity to determine best placement for required monitoring or need for respiratory support. Acute respiratory failure that is life-threatening is defined as RR >24 bpm; using accessory respiratory muscles; acute changes in mental status (confusion, lethargy, coma); hypoxia not improved with supplemental oxygen via Venturi mask or requiring FiO2 >40%; hypercarbia (PaCO2 increased over baseline or elevated >60 mmHG or in the presence of acidosis (pH <=7.25).

Indications for admission or transfer to an Intensive Care Unit per GOLD 2024 include severe dyspnea not responding to initial emergency management, changes in mental status, persistent or worsening hypoxemia and/or hypercarbia despite ventilator support, changes in mental status (confusion, lethargy, coma), need for invasive mechanical ventilation, or hemodynamic instability (need for vasopressors, presence of cardiac arrythmias).

One RCT and a recent Cochrane review found that hospital-at-home care vs. inpatient care for elderly patients with COPD had similar effectiveness at a lower cost while reducing readmission at 6 months and improving depression and quality of life; however, such patients were carefully selected and this may not be an option for the majority of patients with acute COPD exacerbations.

In the most recent RCT including 91 frail, elderly patients presenting to the ED with conditions requiring hospital care, including COPD, patients randomized to hospital-at-home care (at least 1 daily physician and 2 daily nurse visits, home ancillary testing and therapies as needed, and telemedicine support) had 38% lower costs, less testing and consultation, similar high satisfaction, and were less likely to be readmitted within 30 days (7% vs. 23%).

No differences in hospital readmission or return visits at 90 days was reported in a noninferiority RCT of 124 patients with mild COPD based on a DECAF score of 0 to 1. The intervention consisted of twice-daily nurse visits; as needed physician consultation by phone; and full therapy options. There was 1 death in each trial arm.

In a follow-up study of elderly patients admitted with non-acidotic acute exacerbation of COPD, 6-month cumulative mortality was 20%. Lower body mass index (BMI), greater overall severity of illness, and higher functional disability were independently predictive of mortality.
In a VA study of over 51,000 patients discharged after an exacerbation of COPD (mean age 69 years), the risk of death at 1 year was 21% and at 5 years was 55%.

In a cohort of patients with a COPD exacerbation admitted to the medical ICU, half had died at one year. Age and hospital length of stay were independent determinants of mortality (area under the operating curve = 0.687). This information may assist in the provision of hospice care.

Patients who presented with a COPD exacerbation and radiological pneumonia (16% in this UK national audit study) had higher inpatient mortality (11% vs. 7%) and 90-day mortality (17% vs. 13%) compared to those admitted without pneumonia in exacerbation of COPD; differences persisted after adjusting for confounding factors.

Among 1343 patients with COPD, the 11.7% with thrombocytosis had higher in-hospital and 1-year mortality rates. An elevated D-dimer also predicted both short-term and long-term survival in patients admitted for exacerbation of COPD (median survival of patients with D-dimer above and below 1.52 mg/L was 9.6 and 62.6 months). Use of aspirin or clopidogrel was associated with a reduction in 1-year mortality (OR 0.63; 95% CI 0.47-0.85).

Use of the DECAF score (Dyspnea, Eosinopenia, Consolidation, Acidemia, and atrial Fibrillation) predicted in-hospital mortality among patients admitted with an acute exacerbation of COPD with an area under the curve of 0.83 (95% CI 0.78-0.87) for the derivation cohort and 0.82 (95% CI 0.77-0.87) in the validation cohort. A DECAF score of 0 to 1 identified low-risk patients who might be suitable for home care or early supported discharge and a DECAF score of 3 to 6 identified high-risk patients who might be appropriate for more aggressive or palliative care.

Several other scoring systems have been developed to predict future COPD exacerbations including the SCOPEX (Score to Predict Short-Term Risk of COPD Exacerbations) and CEX-HScore (CopdEX-Health Search Score). SCOPEX factors include number of COPD maintenance medications, higher average daily reliever use, greater number of previous year exacerbations, lower FEV1/FVC ratio, and female sex. CEX-HScore was developed in a primary care population including 63,763 patients aged 45 years or older with COPD followed from 2013-2021 until occurrence of an exacerbation. These investigators found 16 factors as determinants of risk of exacerbation over 6 months with a discrimination accuracy of 66% (95% CI 65-67 %) and explained variation of 10% (95% CI 9-11 %).
GOLD 2026 does not recommend use of these scores based on lack of validation and relatively poor test characteristics.

The 4-minute gait speed independently predicts the risk of readmission in older patients hospitalized for acute exacerbation of COPD. Rates of all-cause readmission at 90 days increased across quartiles of decreasing gait speed (fastest: 11.5% to slowest: 48.2%). A multivariate model incorporating 4-minute gait speed, Charlson Index, hospital admission in past year, FEV1% predicted and number of exacerbations in past year predicted 90-day readmission with a C-statistic of 0.86.

Authors of a meta-analysis of 46 investigating readmission for acute exacerbation of COPD identified the following risk factors: male sex; number of hospitalizations in the previous year; hospital length of stay; and comorbidities such as heart failure, tumor or cancer, and diabetes.
Prolonged exacerbation symptom duration is associated with a greater risk of a new exacerbation.

Lower levels of dyspnea, fatigue, and anxiety and higher levels of physical activity are associated with a lower risk of exacerbations but this information does not lead to clearly improved prediction when added to established predictors of exacerbations.

Patients with an acute exacerbation of COPD and eosinophilia may have a a better clinical outcome than those without eosinophilia with respect to length of hospital stay, in-hospital mortality, FEV1, and risk of arrhythmias.

Although considered good clinical practice, there is a lack of evidence supporting a particular program for post-exacerbation follow-up. GOLD 2026 guidelines recommend follow-up at 1 to 4 weeks to assess symptoms (using CAT or mMRC), coping, treatment understanding and adherence, inhaler technique, exercise capacity and ability to perform activities of daily living, status of comorbidities, and need for long-term oxygen.

In a retrospective cohort study of 195 patients discharged following an admission for COPD exacerbation, lack of follow-up with a pulmonologist within 30 days of admission, which occurred in 55.9%, resulted in a significantly increased risk of rehospitalization within 90 days of discharge (OR 2.91; 95% CI 1.06-8.01). There were many reasons that patients failed to return for follow-up, however, making conclusions based on these data problematic.

Follow-up again at 3-4 months is recommended by GOLD 2026 guidelines to reassess the above factors plus measure spirometry (FEV1). Prognosis can also be assessed using validated scoring systems such as BODE.

cell.label: Patient with acute exacerbation of COPD. Meets criteria to hospitalize (e.g., severe symptoms such as sudden worsening of resting dyspnea or acute respiratory failure, onset of new physical signs like cyanosis, failure to respond to initial management, significant comorbidities, new arrhythmia, or insufficient home support)?
Admit and measure ABG. PaO2 <60 mm Hg, moderate to severe acidosis (pH <7.36), plus hypercapnia (PaCO2.45-60 mm Hg) on room air?
Short-acting bronchodilators, short-course oral steroids, and antibiotics.
Low systolic BP and/or no improvement in PaO2 with oxygen.
Oxygen, trial of NIV, and consider mechanical ventilation. Improved?
Admit to ICU if life-threatening exacerbation or requiring mechanical ventilation.
Consider BNP, ECG, and echocardiogram; treat if positive.
Suspect PE; test and treat if positive.
Measure oxygen saturation or ABG. SaO2 <90% and/or PaO2 <60 mm Hg on room air?
Short-acting inhaled bronchodilators and close follow-up. If moderate to severe COPD (FEV1 <50%), add short-course oral steroids.

footnotes.footnote: ABG, arterial blood gas; BP, blood pressure; BNP, blood natriuretic peptide; NIPPV, noninvasive positive pressure ventilation; PE, pulmonary embolism.
